title: Net Effective Rent Explained: Incentives, Cash Payments and Double Counting
metaTitle: Net Effective Rent Example Commercial Leases | YOS
metaDescription: Understand a simple incentive-adjusted rent example, distinguish rent cash payments from contributions, and avoid double counting in your commercial lease comparison.
excerpt: An adjusted rent figure depends on its method. Follow a clearly labelled example and keep actual rent payments, project contributions and the whole occupancy budget separate.
author: Joe Kelley
body:
## What does net effective rent tell you?

An effective rent measure adjusts a rent comparison for incentives using a stated method. It is useful only when the period, inclusions, assumptions and treatment of each incentive are clear. It is not automatically the actual rent cash paid or the total cost of occupying the premises.

This guide uses a simple undiscounted incentive-adjusted average for explanation. It is not a professional valuation method, verified market benchmark or financial advice. Other analyses may treat timing, reviews, contributions and discounting differently; ask the appointed adviser which method suits your decision.

## State the illustrative assumptions first

The following numbers are invented for arithmetic illustration, not Newcastle market rents, an available offer or an example of a YOS client result.

- Floor area: 500 sqm.
- Scheduled face rent: $400 per sqm per year.
- Term: five years, with no rent reviews in this example.
- Rent-free adjustment: three months at the stated rent.
- Separate landlord contribution: $50,000, assumed fully available for eligible project costs in this example.
- All amounts exclude GST. Outgoings, other occupancy costs, tax, financing and the time value of money are excluded.

## Calculate the components once

| Component | Calculation | Illustrative result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduled annual rent before incentives | 500 × $400 | $200,000 |
| Scheduled five-year rent before incentives | $200,000 × 5 | $1,000,000 |
| Rent-free adjustment | $200,000 × 3 ÷ 12 | $50,000 |
| Actual rent cash payments in this example | $1,000,000 − $50,000 | $950,000 |
| Adjusted amount after the separate contribution | $950,000 − $50,000 | $900,000 |
| Simple adjusted annual average | $900,000 ÷ 5 | $180,000 |
| Simple adjusted rent per sqm per year | $180,000 ÷ 500 | $360 |

The tenant pays $950,000 in rent under these assumptions. The $900,000 figure is an incentive-adjusted economic comparison amount after the separate contribution; it is not the rent payment total. The average does not show when rent or project payments occur.

**Helpful tip:** if your starting rent schedule already excludes rent-free periods, use that schedule and do not deduct the same period again.

## Avoid counting the contribution twice

Suppose the same illustration also includes $100,000 of eligible project expenditure and the assumed $50,000 contribution is applied against it. Two consistent presentations give the same combined amount:

- Actual rent cash payments of $950,000 plus net project expenditure of $50,000 equals $1,000,000.
- Incentive-adjusted rent amount of $900,000 plus gross project expenditure of $100,000 equals $1,000,000.

Combining $900,000 of adjusted rent with the already-net $50,000 project cost would produce $950,000 and count the contribution twice. These examples exclude all the other costs listed above and do not establish the total budget for a real lease.

**Helpful tip:** choose one treatment for each benefit, retain the gross figures and show the reconciliation. In a real proposal, check contribution conditions, eligibility, timing and documentation with your advisers.

## Compare more than the adjusted rent

A lower adjusted average does not determine which premises to choose. The comparison also needs the actual review provisions, applicable outgoings, initial works, furniture, technology, moving, existing lease exit obligations and the business fit of the property.

Have your solicitor explain the lease wording and your accountant or appointed financial adviser check tax, cash-flow and accounting assumptions. Do not treat an unconfirmed incentive as an approved budget input.

[Use the full commercial lease comparison checklist](/blog/how-to-compare-commercial-leases)

[Organise inputs in the lease comparison tool](/resources/lease-comparison)

## Connect rent incentives with the workplace scope

If an offer includes a FitOut contribution, define the proposed work and who provides each input. A contribution does not itself establish the actual project scope, contractor appointment or readiness of the building.

[Explore client-side FitOut planning](/office-fitout) and [prepare the budget scope](/blog/office-fitout-cost-guide-australia-2026). YOS coordinates the agreed client workstream; appointed contractors perform construction and trade work.

## Discuss your lease comparison

[Explore Newcastle tenant representation](/tenant-rep/newcastle) or [compare Tenant Rep packages](/tenant-rep#packages). Market comparables are included across the current packages; the agreed scope and evidence limitations still need to be understood.

[Start a free Lease Health Check](/lease-health-check) with the lease situation and timing you know. Uploading your current lease is optional and further advisory work is scoped separately.

[Send your leasing enquiry](#blog-contact-form) with the proposed terms, calculation assumptions and questions that need resolving.

## Sources and method limits

The arithmetic above is a defined illustration, not a rate or formula endorsed by the sources below. RICS discusses adjustment of comparable evidence as part of professional valuation work. NSW retail leasing guidance is contextual; ask your solicitor whether specific rules apply to your premises.

[RICS: valuation approaches and methods](https://www.rics.org/content/rics/uk/en/journals/property-journal/apc-5-valuation-methods.html)

[NSW Small Business Commissioner: leasing costs](https://www.smallbusiness.nsw.gov.au/help/common-questions/understanding-the-costs-of-leasing)
